title: Russian money is flowing through Czech banks. The country lacks a law to seize it
content:
The Czech investigative outlet Investigace.cz has reported that Deutsche Bank severed ties with three Czech banks in 2018 and 2019 over concerns about opaque deposits. Czechia still lacks an effective tool to deal with similar cases.

Lukáš Kraus, an analyst at the Resilient Czechia (Odolné Česko) initiative, which brings together experts on various areas of public administration, has highlighted the issue. Czechia is still awaiting legislation implementing the EU directive on asset recovery and confiscation.

The country has therefore missed the deadline for transposing the EU rules into national law. The government approved the draft legislation in early February and shortly afterwards sent it to the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of parliament. MPs are expected to take it up during the current parliamentary session.

Czechia could face financial penalties for the delayed transposition. The Court of Justice of the EU can impose fines, potentially amounting to hundreds of thousands of euros.

title: EU Budget 2028–2034: What Is Romania Fighting For?
content:
Romania believes that the EU’s new priorities, such as defence, security and industrial competitiveness, should not come at the expense of resources allocated to economic, social and territorial cohesion or agriculture.

To defend Cohesion Policy, President Nicușor Dan joined forces with the Italian Prime Minister to establish the Friends of Cohesion, a group of 17 EU member states which reaffirmed on Thursday their “need for unity and firm determination to put an end to the logic of cuts”. 

Their aim is to sustain the EU’s internal convergence process and preserve the level of ambition of the budget proposal, including its new political priorities and dimensions, as initially presented by the European Commission last summer, Presidential Adviser Valentin Naumescu explained.

President Nicușor Dan argued that one of the group’s objectives had already been “achieved”, as the reduction in national allocations was “insignificant”, even though European Council President António Costa’s proposal envisages cuts of more than 10% compared with the European Commission’s proposal.

title: Black Sea on the Edge: How Romania, Bulgaria and NATO Can Protect Shipping and Critical Infrastructure
content:
Recent incidents show that threats can affect shipping routes, ports and economic interests well beyond the immediate area of military confrontation. An analysis of the Romanian think tank New Strategy Center examines the risks facing the region and outlines the measures needed to strengthen maritime security, protect critical infrastructure and improve deterrence through national, regional and Allied cooperation.

The central message is that securing the Black Sea requires more than isolated national responses. It demands capable coastal states, practical regional cooperation and sustained support from NATO and the European Union.

  • The threat is regional, not merely national
  • Romania needs stronger maritime defence capabilities
  • Bulgaria must reinforce surveillance and response capabilities
  • Türkiye is a key regional security partner
  • NATO needs a more coordinated and persistent Black Sea presence
  • The EU has an important complementary role

title: Pentagon blocks Patriot missile deliveries to Ukraine despite European funding
content:
The order, comprising around 40 PAC-3 missiles and 20 older PAC-2 interceptors, was funded by Kyiv’s Western partners under the PURL initiative. These missiles are Ukraine’s most effective means of defence against Russian ballistic missiles. According to Reuters, citing three people familiar with the matter, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is responsible for the delay.

The delivery schedule called for eight PAC-3 missiles in September, ten in October, ten in November and a further twelve in December. The Pentagon has yet to authorise any of the four shipments. Around 20 older PAC-2 missiles purchased for Ukraine are also awaiting approval for transfer.

The Patriot system and its PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles are largely manufactured in the United States. Germany also produces some PAC-2 missiles. Ukraine or its Western allies have already paid for some of the weapons ordered, and missiles have been placed in storage, including at facilities in Europe.

title: Will chatbots and influencers shape how we vote?
content:
James Talarico, a Democrat running for a US Senate seat in Texas, found an unusual way to distinguish himself from his rivals. His campaign ads carried a message informing viewers that they had been made by humans, not artificial intelligence. Just a few years ago, such a declaration would have made little sense. Today, it has become a political selling point.

Republicans used AI-generated content to attack Talarico. Sensing unease among some voters about such practices, he joined the chorus of criticism of artificial intelligence, turning it into an asset for his own campaign.

“Republicans depicted Democratic candidates and politicians saying all sorts of shocking things in an attempt to create a negative narrative. Interestingly, 70% of these AI-generated ads were not labelled as such. That shows just how fine the line between political advertising and disinformation had become,” says Magdalena Górnicka-Partyka, an expert on election campaigns and US politics and author of Co po Trumpie? Ameryka na rozdrożu (What comes after Trump? America at a crossroads).

title: Hungary’s rule-of-law reset: Did Brussels enable corruption under Orbán?
content:
Six months have passed since the Tisza party, led by former MEP Péter Magyar, won Hungary’s parliamentary elections, ending 16 years of rule by Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party. Upon taking office, Magyar pledged comprehensive reforms to restore the rule of law. It was a promise similar to the one made by Donald Tusk after his electoral victory and the removal of the Law and Justice (PiS) party from power in 2023.

During Orbán’s years in power, Hungary became one of the main sources of contention with EU institutions. The European Commission and the European Parliament repeatedly accused the previous government of undermining judicial independence, politicising the media, restricting minority rights and tolerating corruption and the use of public funds to build political influence.

As a result, Brussels launched proceedings against Budapest under Article 7 of the Treaty on European Union and froze access to EU funds. The new government has already succeeded in securing the release of some of those funds.

title: Czechia changes rules for social media. But its implementation of the DSA may conflict with EU law
content:
Social media platforms, online marketplaces and search engines all fall under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA), which imposes a range of obligations on them. These include making it easier for users to report illegal content, ensuring greater transparency in content moderation and allowing users to appeal certain decisions made by platforms.

Czechia’s Digital Economy Act sets out how compliance with the EU regulation will be monitored and enforced at national level. Czech MPs approved the legislation recently. Its provisions changed several times during the drafting process, both during consultations with experts and as a result of amendments proposed by MPs.

The Czech Telecommunications Office (CTO) will play a key role in overseeing compliance with the DSA, becoming the country’s Digital Services Coordinator. The Chamber of Deputies also added a provision requiring supervisory authorities to take freedom of expression and the right to access information into account when making decisions.

title: Fact check: How NATO was blamed for the vandalism of a Jesus statue in Vilnius
content:
Last week, reports emerged that a gold-coloured statue of Jesus had been removed from a wooden cross mounted on the courtyard wall of the Church of Divine Mercy, carried out into the street and smashed.

A video circulating on social media shows a man carrying the statue after removing it from the cross, while another man films the incident and laughs. The statue eventually falls onto the paving stones and breaks. The men involved quickly left the scene.

Lithuanian media reported that the police were notified of the incident at 00.47 on the 12th of November. On the 14th of November, law enforcement officers managed to establish the identity of the suspected perpetrator.

The suspect is a British national born in 1989 who was visiting Lithuania temporarily. However, following the incident, a precautionary measure was imposed on him – his identity document was confiscated, meaning that he is currently unable to leave Lithuania.

A pre-trial investigation has been launched into the desecration of a grave or another public memorial site.

title: The latest on Warsaw’s push for a permanent US military base in Poland
content:
There are currently around 10 000 US troops stationed in Poland. Most of them are deployed on a rotational basis, but Warsaw wants to ensure that some of this contingent remains in the country permanently. At present, only six European countries host permanent US military bases: Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, Spain, Turkey, and Belgium.

Following talks in Washington with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, Poland’s defence minister said on Tuesday, the 10th of November, that his American counterpart had assured him that “everything is moving in the right direction”.

“In our understanding, this means that the Pentagon has given the green light to a permanent US military base in Poland,” Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said, although the project has yet to receive official US approval.

The Pentagon did not directly confirm that the military base would be established, nor did it confirm the previously reported December deadline for a decision. However, in its comments, it acknowledged that discussions were continuing on strengthening the US military presence in Poland.

title: UK and EU strike three key deals, but thorny issues remain
content:
A decade after the Brexit referendum, London and Brussels are seeking to rebuild a relationship that for years has been marked by disputes over borders, trade and regulation. Today’s (20 November) EU-UK summit delivered tangible results in several key areas.

Negotiations were concluded on three agreements covering opportunities for young people to work and study, measures to facilitate food trade, and the linking of emissions trading systems. Timetables for their implementation were also agreed. Before the new rules can come into force, however, the agreements still need to be formally concluded.

“It has been 10 years since Brexit, but I think today we can all say with confidence that this is a good day for Britain and a good day for Europe. The agreement we have reached together benefits both sides and meets the expectations of the British people,” the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said after the summit.

However, disputes over student tuition fees and cooperation in the electricity market remain unresolved. London is also still seeking assurances that British companies will not lose out as a result of EU plans to support European industry.
